content: The temporomandibular joint (TMJ) is the joint of the jaw, commonly referred to as TMJ. There are two TMJs, one on each side of the face, functioning together. The name temporomandibular is derived from the two bones that form the joint: the temporal bone of the skull and the mandible, or lower jawbone. A unique feature of the TMJ is the presence of an articular disc, which is made of fibrocartilaginous tissue. This disc is positioned between the two bones of the joint and serves as a cushion, allowing smooth movement. The TMJ is one of the few synovial joints in the human body that includes an articular disc, with another example being the sternoclavicular joint. The disc divides the TMJ into two compartments: the lower compartment, which facilitates rotational movements (such as opening and closing the mouth), and the upper compartment, which allows translational movements (such as sliding the jaw forward or side-to-side). The mandibular condyle articulates with the underside of the disc, while the temporal bone articulates with the upper surface of the disc. Pain or dysfunction of the TMJ is often referred to as TMJ, but this term technically refers to the joint itself. The correct term for disorders affecting the TMJ is temporomandibular joint disorder (TMD). TMD encompasses a range of issues involving the TMJ, as well as the associated muscles, tendons, ligaments, blood vessels, and other tissues. Some practitioners may also include the neck, back, or even the entire body when describing problems related to the TMJ. The TMJ is classified as a ginglymoarthrodial joint, meaning it has both hinge-like (ginglymoid) and sliding (arthrodial) movements. The mandibular condyle articulates with the mandibular fossa of the temporal bone, a concave depression in the squamous portion of the temporal bone. These two bones are separated by the articular disc, which divides the joint into two distinct compartments. The inferior compartment allows pure rotation of the condylar head, corresponding to the initial 20 mm of mouth opening. Beyond this point, further opening of the mouth requires activation of the superior compartment, where the condylar head and articular disc translate forward within the glenoid fossa and down the articular eminence of the temporal bone. This anterior movement facilitates further mouth opening. The TMJ has six main components: the mandibular condyles, the articular surface of the temporal bone, the joint capsule, the articular disc, the ligaments, and the lateral pterygoid muscle. The joint capsule is a fibrous membrane that surrounds the joint and incorporates the articular eminence. It attaches to the articular eminence, the articular disc, and the neck of the mandibular condyle. The articular disc, a fibrous extension of the capsule, functions as an articulating surface against both the temporal bone and the condyles, dividing the joint into two sections. The disc is biconcave in structure and attaches medially and laterally to the condyle. Its anterior portion splits vertically to accommodate the insertion of the superior head of the lateral pterygoid muscle, while the posterior portion also splits vertically, forming the retrodiscal tissue. Unlike the disc itself, the retrodiscal tissue is vascularized and innervated, and pain during mandibular movement in cases of anterior disc displacement is often due to compression of this tissue by the condyle. The TMJ is supported by three ligaments: one major ligament (the temporomandibular ligament) and two minor ligaments (the stylomandibular and sphenomandibular ligaments). The temporomandibular ligament is the thickened lateral portion of the capsule and has two parts: an outer oblique portion (OOP) and an inner horizontal portion (IHP). The stylomandibular ligament separates the infratemporal region from the parotid region and extends from the styloid process to the angle of the mandible. The sphenomandibular ligament runs from the spine of the sphenoid bone to the lingula of the mandible. These ligaments define the limits of mandibular movements, and movements beyond these functional limits often result in painful stimuli. Sensory innervation of the TMJ is provided by the auriculotemporal and masseteric branches of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (V3). The joint's arterial blood supply is primarily derived from branches of the external carotid artery, particularly the superficial temporal artery. Other contributing branches include the deep auricular artery, anterior tympanic artery, ascending pharyngeal artery, and maxillary artery. Proprioception within the TMJ involves four types of receptors: Ruffini endings (static mechanoreceptors for mandibular positioning), Pacinian corpuscles (dynamic mechanoreceptors for movement acceleration), Golgi tendon organs (static mechanoreceptors for ligament protection), and free nerve endings (pain receptors for joint protection). The central portion of the articular disc lacks innervation and vascularization, which prevents pain and bleeding during jaw movements. During jaw movements, only the mandible moves. Normal mandibular movements during functions like chewing are called excursions, which include lateral excursions (left and right) and forward excursion (protrusion). The reversal of protrusion is called retrusion. Protrusion involves the mandibular incisors moving edge-to-edge with the maxillary incisors and then surpassing them, creating a temporary underbite. This movement is achieved by translation of the condyle down the articular eminence in the upper TMJ compartment, with minimal rotation in the lower compartment. Chewing involves specific mandibular movements dictated by the two TMJs. The side of the mandible that moves laterally is referred to as the working or rotating side, while the opposite side is the balancing or orbiting side. During lateral excursions, the working-side condyle rotates horizontally, while the balancing-side condyle translates. Functional chewing incorporates both side-to-side and up-and-down movements, with rotation in the vertical plane occurring in both condyles. The mandible is primarily moved by the four muscles of mastication: the masseter, medial pterygoid, lateral pterygoid, and temporalis. These muscles, all innervated by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (V3), work in groups to move the mandible in different directions. The lateral pterygoid muscle pulls the disc and condyle forward within the glenoid fossa and down the articular eminence, facilitating mouth opening. The masseter, medial pterygoid, and temporalis muscles close the mouth by pulling the mandible upward. The most common TMJ disorder is disc displacement, where the articular disc moves out of its normal position between the condyle and the fossa. This displacement often causes pain because the central portion of the disc lacks sensory innervation, unlike the surrounding tissues. In most cases, the disc is displaced anteriorly during translation of the condyle. A pop or click sound may occur when the condyle moves back onto the disc (disc displacement with reduction). Upon closing, the condyle may slide off the back of the disc, causing another click or pop. In cases of disc displacement without reduction, the disc remains anterior to the condyle during opening, limiting mouth opening and eliminating the pop or click sounds. TMJ pain can result from myofascial pain dysfunction syndrome (involving the muscles of mastication), internal derangements (such as disc displacement), or degenerative joint disease (osteoarthritis). TMJ pain is also a reliable diagnostic criterion for temporal arteritis.
